column1: 01.01|Start by naming the actors, operations, and promises. For a short link, creation and redirect are separate operations with different latency and correctness needs.|Write down ownership, retention, access rules, traffic, and what happens when a dependency fails before choosing infrastructure.

01.02|Draw the path from request to durable state and back. Keep the diagram at the level of responsibilities until the data flow is clear.|Mark the source of truth, synchronous calls, and any background work; a box without a reason to exist can wait.

01.03|Turn “fast” and “reliable” into measurable targets, such as p99 latency, monthly availability, recovery time, and data loss tolerance.|Measure the user-visible operation, not only the health of one service.

01.04|Every design buys one property with another: latency with memory, isolation with coordination, or simplicity with limited scale.|State the workload and failure mode that justify each tradeoff, then record when the choice should be revisited.

01.05|Availability is the ability to answer, durability is the survival of accepted data, consistency is agreement about its value, and cost limits every plan.|Specify the promise per operation; a read and a payment commit may need very different priorities.

01.06|Convert daily volume to average and peak requests per second, then estimate bytes per record, replication, indexes, and retention.|Keep units visible. Add headroom for bursts, but do not turn rough assumptions into false precision.

01.07|A server can overlap I/O-bound requests with event loops or threads, while CPU work still needs cores or workers.|Set concurrency limits against memory and downstream capacity; unlimited in-flight requests become a queue inside the process.

01.08|Vertical scaling increases one machine’s resources; horizontal scaling adds machines and forces shared-state decisions.|Scale the bottleneck shown by measurements, then plan for the point where one host becomes an availability risk.

01.09|A monolith keeps transactions and deployment simple; services offer independent ownership and scaling at the price of network failure.|Split along stable business boundaries when team and deployment pressure make that cost worthwhile.

01.10|A repository keeps domain code focused on operations such as save and find while hiding storage details.|Do not hide query shape or transaction boundaries so completely that callers cannot reason about cost and correctness.

01.11|Model stable identities and relationships first, then leave explicit extension points for fields that will change.|Validate extensions and version their meaning; an unbounded JSON column can become a schema nobody understands.

01.12|Compare cost per successful operation at expected and peak load, including storage, transfer, replicas, and staff time.|Prefer a simpler component when its capacity margin is sufficient; unused resilience still has a bill.

01.13|New infrastructure adds deployment, monitoring, recovery, and expertise obligations.|Use the smallest system that satisfies measured requirements; define the trigger that would justify adding the next component.

02.01|An API contract names resources or operations, input validation, errors, pagination, and compatibility rules.|Make retries and side effects explicit; clients need to know whether repeating a call is safe.

02.02|A remote call crosses a failure boundary even when both services run in one cluster.|Budget timeouts across the whole request, propagate context, and choose which failures can be handled asynchronously.

02.03|HTTP is the transport, REST is a resource-oriented style, and gRPC provides typed RPC contracts over HTTP/2.|Choose by client ecosystem, streaming needs, and evolution costs rather than treating one protocol as inherently faster.

02.04|TCP preserves ordered reliable bytes; UDP leaves delivery and ordering to the application and can reduce handshake overhead.|Use UDP when the application can tolerate or repair loss, as in real-time media; use TCP for ordinary business requests.

02.05|A gateway enforces cross-cutting API policies, while a load balancer distributes traffic among healthy backends.|Place authentication and quotas at the correct trust boundary; avoid duplicating policy across layers.

02.06|A load balancer selects healthy targets with round robin, least connections, or a workload-aware policy.|Health checks should test readiness, and draining should let in-flight requests finish before removing a target.
02.07|Consistent hashing keeps related keys on a stable subset of servers when membership changes.|Virtual nodes smooth uneven distribution, but hot keys still need a separate mitigation.

02.08|An event contract defines identity, schema, occurrence time, producer, and version—not just a payload name.|Consumers must tolerate duplicates and compatible schema evolution because events may outlive the producer’s deployment.

02.09|Set a bounded timeout, retry only recoverable failures, and use an idempotency key for side-effecting requests.|Persist the result against the key so a retry after a lost response does not repeat the effect.
02.10|Batching amortizes network and storage overhead across multiple items.|Bound both batch size and wait time; a large batch can improve throughput while making individual requests slower.
02.11|Backpressure tells producers when consumers cannot keep up.|Use bounded queues, credits, or rejection; an unbounded buffer merely postpones overload until memory runs out.

02.12|The slowest requests shape p99 latency and user experience even when the mean looks healthy.|Measure each dependency and queue separately; a fanout request amplifies the chance of encountering a slow tail.
02.13|Load shedding refuses lower-priority work before overload collapses every request.|Choose priorities and an explicit response, and keep the admission decision ahead of expensive work.

03.01|Start relational design with entities, keys, cardinality, and invariants enforced by constraints.|Normalize for correctness, then denormalize only for a measured read pattern with a clear update path.

03.02|A SQL-backed key-value store needs a unique key, value representation, version or timestamp, and clear overwrite semantics.|Index the lookup key and decide whether writes are insert-only, conditional, or last-write-wins.
03.03|An index trades write and storage cost for a faster access path.|Index predicates and sort order used by real queries; check plans rather than indexing every column.

03.04|A B-tree keeps sorted keys in pages, supporting point lookups and ranges with logarithmic navigation.|Page locality and key order matter; a random write pattern may cost more than a sequential one.
03.05|A planner estimates row counts and chooses scans, joins, and indexes.|Compare estimated with actual rows using EXPLAIN ANALYZE; stale statistics often explain surprising plans.
03.06|Locks and isolation decide what concurrent transactions may observe or modify.|Keep transactions short and test conflicting writes; isolation names alone do not prove an application invariant.
03.07|MVCC lets readers see a stable snapshot while writers create newer row versions.|Old versions need cleanup, and long-running transactions can prevent that cleanup from advancing.

03.08|A write-ahead log records changes before data pages are flushed so committed work can be replayed after a crash.|Check the durability settings and recovery path; a successful API response should have a defined persistence point.
03.09|A ticket server allocates ranges of identifiers to writers to avoid a centralized call per row.|Range leasing improves throughput but leaves gaps on crashes; use it only if gaps are acceptable.

03.10|Scale SQL by improving queries and indexes, then add replicas or partitioning where the measured bottleneck demands it.|Replicas make reads stale, and sharding complicates joins and transactions; quantify the benefit first.
03.11|Online index creation reduces blocking while a table remains in use.|Budget extra disk and I/O, monitor progress, and keep a rollback plan for a slow or failed build.
03.12|Use expand, migrate, contract: add compatible fields, backfill, switch readers and writers, then remove old fields.|Deployments overlap, so both schema versions must work during the transition.
03.13|Soft deletion records a removal state while retaining rows for recovery or audit.|Apply the predicate consistently to reads, uniqueness rules, and eventual purge jobs.

04.01|Choose a non-relational store for an access pattern or scale property it actually serves, not for a vague promise of flexibility.|Write down required queries, transaction boundaries, and consistency before selecting a data model.

04.02|Document stores group related fields into one retrievable object; key-value stores excel when the key is known.|Large mutable documents and secondary queries change the cost profile; model the update path as well as the read.

04.03|Columnar storage groups values by column for analytic scans; wide-column stores partition rows by key for operational access.|Their similar names hide different workloads, so start with query shape and update frequency.

04.04|A graph database is useful when relationship traversal is the main operation and depth is not known in advance.|For shallow, fixed joins, relational indexes may be simpler and faster to operate.
04.05|Partitioning divides data or work by a key so one node does not own everything.|Pick a key that distributes load and supports common queries; cross-partition operations become more expensive.
04.06|A hot partition appears when one key or range receives disproportionate traffic.|Measure per-key load; salting, write spreading, or isolating a celebrity key can restore balance.
04.07|Hash keys onto a ring so adding a node remaps only part of the keyspace.|Replicas and virtual nodes improve balance, but placement changes still need controlled migration.

04.08|Distributed IDs can use random values, leased ranges, or time plus worker and sequence bits.|Decide whether order, compactness, predictability, and offline generation matter before choosing a scheme.

04.09|UUIDs favor decentralized uniqueness, ObjectIds embed time and process information, and Snowflake-style IDs use sortable time bits.|Ordering is only approximate when clocks drift; do not use an ID as proof of causality.

04.10|A Snowflake ID packs timestamp, worker ID, and per-time-unit sequence into one integer.|Handle clock rollback and sequence exhaustion explicitly, or duplicate and out-of-order IDs become possible.
04.11|Clock skew can move a generated timestamp backward even while events continue forward.|Use logical sequence or database order for correctness; treat wall-clock order as an estimate.
04.12|Keyset pagination resumes after the last sort key instead of skipping an ever-growing offset.|Use a unique tie-breaker and preserve the filter and sort order in the cursor.
04.13|A Bloom filter can prove absence but only suggest presence.|Size it for expected items and false-positive rate; still check the source of truth after a positive answer.
04.14|Keep frequently accessed data on a fast path and archive older data to cheaper storage.|Define retrieval time and retention promises before moving records out of the primary store.

05.01|Caches can sit in a browser, CDN, service process, or distributed store; each has a different scope and invalidation problem.|Name the authoritative store and the maximum acceptable staleness for each cached value.
05.02|A distributed cache shares hot data across service instances and can reduce database read load.|Partition keys, set memory limits, and plan for eviction or a full cache outage.

05.03|LRU favors recently used keys, LFU favors frequent keys, and size-aware policies protect memory better when objects vary.|Compare hit rate under real traffic; an algorithm name is not a substitute for workload measurement.
05.04|TTL bounds how long stale entries survive without explicit invalidation.|Add jitter to large groups of expirations, and remember that a reaper may delete later than the logical expiry.

05.05|When many requests miss the same key, one should load it while others wait or use stale data.|Bound the wait and cache negative results carefully to avoid turning one miss into a database stampede.
05.06|A cache outage should have a deliberate fallback policy, not an accidental flood to the database.|Use admission limits or serve stale values when allowed; measure fallback capacity in advance.

06.01|Distributed nodes communicate through a network that can delay, duplicate, reorder, or lose messages.|Describe the fault model before promising coordination; a timeout only proves that no answer arrived in time.

06.02|Strong consistency makes newer writes visible according to a defined order; eventual consistency permits temporary divergence.|Pick the model per operation and state what a client may observe after its own write.
06.03|Replication copies data for availability or read capacity, but replicas can lag or disagree.|Define acknowledgement quorum, failover rules, and repair of divergent copies.

06.04|CAP describes the choice during a partition; PACELC adds latency versus consistency while the network is healthy.|Tie the theorem to a concrete read or write path instead of labeling an entire product with two letters.

06.05|Physical clocks estimate time; logical clocks capture order or causality without trusting synchronized wall time.|Use a sequence, version, or Lamport clock when the application needs ordering guarantees.
06.06|Consensus lets a group agree on a sequence despite some node failures.|It needs a quorum and has a latency cost; place it around metadata or critical state, not every cache hit.
06.07|Leader election gives one node authority to coordinate a task for a term.|Use a term or epoch on its writes so an old leader cannot continue acting after losing leadership.
06.08|A lease expires if not renewed, allowing another worker to take ownership.|Protect the resource with a fencing token; a paused worker may resume after its lease has expired.
06.09|A Redis lock can reduce overlap, but lock ownership alone cannot stop a delayed former owner.|Pass increasing fencing tokens to the protected storage system and reject stale tokens there.

06.10|Circuit breakers stop repeated calls to an unhealthy dependency and probe for recovery later.|Pair them with bounded timeouts and fallback behavior; an open breaker should fail quickly and visibly.

06.11|Gossip spreads membership or state through periodic peer exchange without a central broadcaster.|Convergence takes time, so do not use gossip as the only source of immediate truth for a critical decision.
06.12|A metadata service maps partitions and services to current owners.|Version the map and handle stale clients during movement; discovery itself needs a reliable bootstrap path.

06.13|A distributed hash table locates keys through peer routing rather than one central index.|Account for churn, replication, and routing hops; the theoretical lookup cost is only part of operational latency.

07.01|A storage engine must balance latency, throughput, durability, write amplification, and device behavior.|List read and write shapes first; the best layout for random point reads differs from one for sequential ingest.

07.02|In-place updates favor some reads; append-oriented designs favor writes and later pay for compaction.|Measure total I/O, not only foreground latency, because maintenance competes with serving traffic.

07.03|A file-backed dictionary can append key-value records and rebuild an in-memory offset index on startup.|Define framing, deletion markers, and crash recovery before treating the file as durable storage.
07.04|A binary format needs a versioned header, length fields, checksums, and an unambiguous byte order.|Reject truncated or corrupt records safely; leave room for readers that lag a writer version.

07.05|Byte-range requests read a selected segment of a large object without transferring the whole file.|Keep an index of offsets and lengths, and make object versions immutable so offsets remain valid.

07.06|Immutable data files let readers hold an old version while writers publish a new one atomically.|Use a manifest or pointer swap, then collect old versions only after readers no longer need them.
07.07|A log-structured store appends new records and resolves the latest value through an index or merge.|Compaction reclaims superseded data, but consumes disk and I/O that must be budgeted.
07.08|Bitcask writes values to an append-only log and keeps key-to-offset pointers in memory.|It offers simple fast point lookups when keys fit in memory; segment merge and crash rebuild need care.
07.09|An LSM tree writes into memory, flushes sorted files, and compacts overlapping files later.|It trades fast sequential writes for read and compaction amplification; tune for the actual workload.

07.10|A memtable holds current writes, a WAL protects them, and SSTables store sorted durable runs.|Recovery replays the WAL after the last durable flush; flush and log truncation must be coordinated.

07.11|Bloom filters skip files that cannot contain a key; sparse indexes locate a nearby block within a sorted file.|False positives still require reads, and checksums should cover blocks returned from disk.
07.12|Compaction merges sorted runs and discards overwritten or expired entries.|Track write amplification, temporary disk space, and stalls when compaction falls behind.

07.13|Object storage stores large blobs cheaply and durably; databases provide indexed records and transactions.|Keep blob bytes and searchable metadata in separate systems with a clear consistency workflow.

07.14|An object store needs a metadata index, data placement, replication or erasure coding, and a read path that locates chunks.|Define how PUT becomes visible and how lost nodes are repaired without losing accepted objects.

07.15|Range partitioning preserves ordered scans but risks hot ranges; hash placement spreads keys but disrupts locality.|Choose according to dominant queries and plan how ownership changes as capacity grows.
07.16|A partition manager records which node owns each partition and coordinates moves.|Publish map versions atomically and let old owners redirect or reject stale requests during handoff.
07.17|Object metadata maps names to versions, locations, sizes, and lifecycle state.|Make metadata durable and scalable; intact blobs are useless if their locating records disappear.
07.18|An append-only stream assigns each record a stable position and advances readers with offsets.|Retention, segment rolling, and consumer lag determine when old data can be removed.

07.19|Durability requires accepted writes to survive the chosen failure set, such as one disk or one availability zone.|Count only acknowledgements from independent failure domains and test recovery from a lost replica.
07.20|Checksums detect corruption across memory, network, disk, and later reads.|Verify at each handoff and retain an independent good copy so detection can lead to repair.

08.01|Move work off a request path when the user does not need its result before receiving a response.|Persist the task before acknowledging it, and expose completion or failure through a status record.

08.02|A task queue gives one worker a job; an event stream lets several consumer groups read the same ordered history.|Choose based on delivery and replay needs, then make each handler safe for repeated delivery.
08.03|A product event bus decouples producers from notifications, analytics, and other readers.|Publish an event only after the underlying state change is durable, often through an outbox.
08.04|Queue lag is the age or count of work waiting for processing.|Alert on the oldest item and estimate catch-up time; worker count alone does not reveal whether users are falling behind.
08.05|A scheduler decides when a job becomes eligible, while workers perform it.|Use durable schedules and a lease or claim protocol so crashes do not silently lose jobs.
08.06|Workers can claim rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and process independent jobs concurrently.|Use a lease or retry state for crashed workers, and keep the claiming transaction short.
08.07|A DAG workflow runs tasks after their dependencies complete.|Persist each step’s state and outputs so a restart can resume without repeating unsafe side effects.
08.08|A rule engine maps events and conditions to actions without embedding every policy in application code.|Version rules, record why a rule fired, and cap recursive triggers to prevent loops.

08.09|Fanout can happen on write, on read, or through a shared log consumed by many downstream services.|A large audience turns eager fanout into a burst; hybrid delivery keeps ordinary users fast without overwhelming the system.
08.10|A flash sale is a contention problem: many buyers compete for a small number of units.|Reserve inventory atomically, expire abandoned holds, and make payment completion idempotent.

09.01|Search has an ingestion path that builds an index and a query path that retrieves and ranks candidates.|Define freshness, relevance, and latency separately; a good index is useless if updates arrive too late.

09.02|An inverted index maps each term to a posting list of document IDs, often with positions and frequencies.|Compression and skip pointers reduce I/O; updates require segment or posting maintenance.
09.03|Boolean retrieval intersects and unions postings; tiered search scans the most promising subset first.|Keep a fallback to broader tiers when the top tier has too few results.
09.04|TF-IDF raises the weight of a term that is frequent in one document but uncommon across the corpus.|Normalize for document length; raw term counts reward long documents unfairly.
09.05|BM25 combines term frequency saturation, inverse document frequency, and length normalization.|Tune it on judged queries and evaluate the whole ranking pipeline, not only the formula.

09.06|Stop words reduce noisy postings, while champion lists keep top candidate documents for common terms.|Over-aggressive pruning can remove meaningful exact matches; preserve a route to complete retrieval.

09.07|A query pipeline normalizes text, detects language, corrects terms, expands intent, and builds candidate requests.|Keep original terms available so a correction does not silently replace a precise user query.

09.08|Clicks and dwell signals can improve ranking, but position bias makes high-ranked results look better even when they are not.|Log exposure and compare against controlled experiments before treating feedback as relevance truth.

09.09|Offline search evaluation compares retrieved results with judged relevant items using precision, recall, NDCG, and related measures.|Pair it with online latency and behavior metrics; a relevance lift that slows every query may not help users.
09.10|A database update and its search-index update are separate writes with a failure gap.|Use an outbox or change stream, track lag, and make indexing idempotent so retries converge.
09.11|Shard an index by document or term to spread storage and query work.|A coordinating node must merge results; skewed shards and cross-shard ranking complicate latency.
09.12|A crawler discovers URLs, fetches pages politely, canonicalizes content, and feeds an indexing pipeline.|Deduplicate, honor crawl policies, and schedule recrawls according to change frequency.

09.13|Vector retrieval finds semantic neighbors; lexical retrieval preserves exact terms, identifiers, and rare names.|Combine candidate sets and rerank, then measure relevance on queries where the methods disagree.

09.14|Autocomplete retrieves likely completions for a prefix under a tight latency budget.|Precompute popular prefixes, filter unsafe or private suggestions, and update popularity without rebuilding everything.
09.15|Spell correction generates plausible edits and ranks them using frequency and context.|Offer the correction without erasing the original query, especially for names, codes, and technical terms.

09.16|Related searches are alternative intents derived from aggregate query behavior or semantic similarity.|Avoid echoing a single user’s private history; rank suggestions by usefulness and diversity.
09.17|Recent searches are a user-scoped ordered history with deletion and retention controls.|Keep private queries out of shared caches and honor clear-history requests across devices.
10.01|Large counters can shard increments by key and time, then merge partial sums for reads.|Specify whether the displayed count must be exact and how late or duplicate events are handled.
10.02|A view is a defined event, not merely a page request; retries and refreshes can inflate it.|Choose deduplication identity and window, then state whether bot and repeated views count.
10.03|An impression should reflect actual exposure, often with viewport and duration criteria.|Emit the event once per eligible display and keep the definition stable across clients.
10.04|HyperLogLog estimates distinct values using compact registers derived from hash patterns.|Its error is statistical; use exact sets for low-cardinality or correctness-critical decisions.
10.05|Mergeable sketches combine summaries from shards without moving every raw event.|Check that the merge operation preserves the metric’s meaning and expected error bound.
10.06|Time buckets turn an unbounded stream into bounded windows that can be added and expired.|Decide how late arrivals update old buckets and whether queries need event time or processing time.
10.07|Raw events preserve the ability to rebuild metrics; aggregates make common queries cheap.|Retain raw data long enough for corrections and document the derivation version of each aggregate.

10.08|A count-min sketch estimates event frequency with small memory and one-sided overcount error.|Use independent hashes and size it for desired error; confirm heavy candidates against exact counts when needed.
10.09|A top-k summary tracks likely heavy hitters without storing every key.|Merge summaries carefully and verify finalists if the product requires exact rankings.
10.10|Reservoir sampling keeps an unbiased fixed-size sample from a stream of unknown length.|Use it for estimation or inspection, not for rare-event guarantees.
10.11|A t-digest stores centroids that approximate quantiles, especially near distribution tails.|Merge digests across workers and validate tail error against known samples.
10.12|Streaming percentile dashboards summarize latency distributions over time windows.|Keep units and aggregation windows consistent; averaging p99 values is not the p99 of all requests.

10.13|Live reactions can absorb bursts in a queue or stream, aggregate briefly, and push compact updates to viewers.|Persist individual reactions if undo and exact counts matter; the live display may tolerate a small delay.

11.01|WebSocket gateways hold many connections while a shared data layer tracks subscriptions and updates.|Partition by connection or topic, limit fanout, and reconnect clients with a cursor after a gateway restart.

11.02|WebSockets support bidirectional messages, SSE streams server events over HTTP, and long polling repeatedly waits for updates.|Choose by direction, browser support, infrastructure, and reconnect behavior.
11.03|Store users, posts, follows, and interactions around the queries the product actually needs.|Separate the authoritative relationship edge from cached counts and derived feed materializations.
11.04|A follow graph is a directed edge set with high-degree celebrities and uneven query patterns.|Index both follower and following directions or keep dedicated views; account for hot nodes.

11.05|Push feeds prefill inboxes, pull feeds assemble them at read time, and hybrid feeds choose per publisher or audience.|Celebrities make push expensive, while pull increases read latency; model both traffic shapes.
11.06|An unread badge compares the newest relevant item with the user’s last-seen position.|Store a monotonic cursor and define whether edits, deletions, and multiple devices change the badge.
11.07|Extract hashtags using a clear tokenizer and keep a tag-to-content index.|Normalize case and Unicode consistently, and update the index when content changes or is removed.
11.08|Model one reaction per user, target, and reaction type with a unique constraint.|Counts are derived and can lag; use idempotent writes and reconcile drift rather than trusting every increment.
11.09|Photo tags need coordinates relative to the original image or a normalized coordinate space.|Transform them during crops and resizing, and enforce who may tag or remove a person.
11.10|Live commentary is an ordered event stream delivered to many connected readers.|Use sequence numbers for reconnect and decide how late edits or corrections appear.
12.01|Nearby search first narrows candidates with a spatial index, then computes accurate distance and ranks them.|Filter by availability and permissions before returning a close but unusable result.
12.02|Geohash turns nearby coordinates into common prefixes at a chosen resolution.|Query adjacent cells too; a close point may cross a cell boundary.

12.03|H3 uses hexagonal cells, S2 uses hierarchical spherical cells, and geohash uses rectangular string prefixes.|Compare coverage, precision, and operational tooling for the actual geographic queries.
12.04|Redis GEO can keep a fast index of current positions for nearby candidate lookup.|Expire stale locations and persist authoritative state elsewhere if positions must survive cache loss.
12.05|Geofencing tests whether a point falls inside a polygon, often after a bounding-box prefilter.|Define behavior at the boundary and use a consistent coordinate system.
12.06|Ray casting counts intersections from a point to outside; odd counts mean inside.|Handle points on edges, vertices, and holes deliberately, because naive intersection rules disagree there.
12.07|A Bloom filter cheaply excludes definitely unseen items but may falsely mark a new item as seen.|Use an exact set when false exclusion is unacceptable, such as a paid entitlement.
12.08|Matching narrows eligible pairs, scores them, then applies capacity and fairness constraints.|Measure outcomes after assignment; the best local score may lead to poor global utilization.

13.01|Give the client a short-lived scoped upload URL so file bytes go directly to object storage.|The application still validates ownership, content metadata, and completion before exposing the object.
13.02|An image CDN caches precomputed or on-demand resized variants near readers.|Bound allowed dimensions and formats, and include transformation parameters in cache keys.
13.03|An avatar service maps a user and image version to stable variant URLs.|Invalidate on change, provide a safe default, and avoid leaking private source images through public variants.
13.04|Multipart upload lets large videos resume parts rather than restarting from zero.|Scope signed URLs to one object and expiry, and verify completed parts and size before accepting metadata.

13.05|A transcoding pipeline reads an uploaded source, produces renditions, packages segments, and publishes a manifest.|Treat each step as retryable and keep the source immutable until all required outputs are checked.

13.06|Adaptive bitrate playback selects segments based on measured throughput and buffer health.|The CDN serves multiple renditions; the client’s switching policy trades picture quality against stalls.

13.07|Signed URLs limit access duration, while DRM manages licensed playback keys; neither replaces application authorization.|Check entitlement before issuing playback credentials and keep key delivery separate from public segments.

13.08|WebRTC prioritizes interactive low latency, while segmented live streaming scales to large audiences with more delay.|Choose the latency target first, then plan ingest, transcoding, distribution, and reconnect behavior.
13.09|File sync compares local and remote versions, transfers changed data, and resolves concurrent edits.|Use version vectors or explicit conflict copies when both sides changed offline.

13.10|Fixed-size chunks simplify addressing and retries; content hashes identify identical bytes for deduplication.|A small insertion shifts many fixed boundaries, so content-defined chunking may save more transfer on edited files.

13.11|A file manifest lists chunk identities and order for one immutable version.|Publish a new manifest atomically, retain shared chunks while referenced, and garbage-collect unreferenced ones later.
14.01|Logs explain events, metrics show trends, and traces connect work across service boundaries.|Propagate correlation IDs and measure the user request from entry to response.

14.02|An SLO defines a target for a user-visible indicator; the error budget is the allowed misses in a window.|Use budget burn to guide release pace and incident priority, not as a substitute for understanding impact.

14.03|Incident response first stabilizes the service, then records a timeline and follows the evidence to causes.|Assign an incident lead and communicate status; review contributing conditions after recovery without blame.
14.04|Safe releases use small batches, health gates, and a reversible switch to the prior version.|Ensure old and new versions coexist with current schemas and messages during rollout.

14.05|Database migrations need compatible schema steps, controlled backfills, and verification of row counts or checksums.|Keep the old read path available until the new one proves correct under real traffic.

14.06|A parallel monolith can receive a gradually increasing share of reads while the old system remains authoritative.|Compare responses, watch latency and errors, then move writes only after semantics are aligned.

14.07|A backup is useful only if a restore can produce consistent, usable data within the required time.|Test restores regularly and record the latest recoverable point, credentials, and dependencies.

14.08|Disaster recovery specifies the tolerated outage and data loss when a region or major dependency fails.|Practice failover and failback; a written plan cannot reveal missing DNS, secrets, or capacity.
14.09|Retention rules define when data must be kept and when it must be deleted from primary stores, replicas, and backups.|Minimize stored personal data and provide an auditable deletion workflow.

14.10|Protect entry points with authentication, authorization, validation, quotas, and abuse signals.|Threat-model high-value operations and keep enforcement close to the resource, not only at the edge.

14.11|Rate-limit keys may be a user, token, IP, tenant, or operation; each captures a different abuse pattern.|Place the limit before expensive work and avoid making shared NAT users block one another.

14.12|A sliding window counts requests within the last duration rather than resetting at a fixed boundary.|Use timestamps or approximated buckets, and make concurrent increments atomic for the promised precision.

14.13|Multi-tenancy shares infrastructure while keeping each tenant’s data, identity, quotas, and configuration separate.|Put tenant identity in every authorization and data access path; test cross-tenant isolation directly.

15.01|On one machine, a URL shortener needs a unique short code, a durable mapping table, and a redirect endpoint.|Use a uniqueness constraint, validate destinations, and define what happens if click tracking fails.

15.02|A rate-limiting service needs a key policy, atomic counters, and a response that tells clients when to retry.|Pair quotas with abuse signals; one global limit can unfairly penalize legitimate bursts.

15.03|At scale, redirect traffic can use caches and read replicas while link creation remains anchored to durable storage.|A disabled link must invalidate or expire cached redirects within the product’s promised window.

15.04|A product listing combines authoritative catalog data, searchable fields, and a price or availability source.|Separate stale browse tolerance from checkout correctness; a card can be cached while inventory cannot be guessed.
15.05|A collaborative editor distributes operations or document states among concurrent clients.|Choose OT or CRDT semantics, persist an operation log, and reconnect clients from a known version.

15.06|An object store separates object metadata from chunk placement and durable data nodes.|Publish a completed object only after required chunks are acknowledged and its metadata points to a recoverable layout.

15.07|A Kafka-style log appends records to partitioned segments and lets consumers track offsets.|Ordering is per partition; leader failover, replication acknowledgements, and retention determine its guarantees.

16.01|A notification system accepts one intent, resolves recipients and preferences, then delivers through channel-specific workers.|Make sends idempotent where possible and retain status for retries, suppression, and user support.
16.02|Ticket booking must hold a seat temporarily, confirm payment, and release abandoned holds.|Make the seat transition atomic so two buyers cannot both receive a confirmed reservation.

16.03|A payment system records an immutable ledger of intents, attempts, and completed transfers.|Idempotency keys and reconciliation handle lost responses; never infer success solely from a client redirect.
16.04|A search service ingests source changes, builds indexes, and serves ranked results through a query coordinator.|Define freshness and fallback behavior when an index shard is missing or behind.

16.05|A recommendation system retrieves eligible candidates, ranks them, and applies diversity or policy constraints.|Log exposures, not only clicks, and plan for new users and new items with little history.
16.06|Chat needs ordered conversations, durable messages, delivery state, and reconnect from a cursor.|Define ordering per conversation and handle duplicate sends with client-generated IDs.

16.07|A social feed combines followed sources, candidate generation, ranking, and a stable pagination cursor.|Use a hybrid push/pull strategy for high-degree accounts and keep privacy changes from leaking old materializations.
